div.p: The process of guaranteeing that real-time somare will meet its timing requirements, is referred to as schedulability analysis. In this paper an implementation independent Schedulability Analysis Tool (SAT) for real-time applications is presented and the supported analysis methods are discussed. U T can be used during the initial stages of the design phase when the effects of the operating system or the runtime system are not considered. However, the methoh supported by the tool are based on an event-action flamework and thus, new events or actions introduced by the underlying sofiare can also be evaluated and included in the performed cmalysis.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A hard real-time system has the dual responsibility of producing correct results and meeting deadlines. Guaranteeing that real-time software will meet its timing requirements, a process well-known as schedulability analysis, is an integral and important part of real-time soilware development.

Schedulability analysis provides guaranteed measures oftiming requirements. However, this kind of a priori verikation, at earlier phases of design, must be complemented with the issues concerning the implementation timing costs and the actual performance pa"&n. In reality, there is a significant gap between the theoretical results and the implementation of realtime scheduling algorithms on systems consisting of real processors and real operating systems.

Although schedulability analysis tools already exist (e.g., Schedulability Analyzer for Real-Time Euclid ill], Flex language [6]), they are language dependent and they have not yet been established as well-known commercial products. A schedulability analysis tool should be, to a certain degree, an implementation-independent tool covering the needs of pre-analysis, during the earlier design phase of a bard real-time application. Such a tool can help application developers tocorrectlyanalyzethetimingbehaviourofthekrealtime system. From this perspective, this tool can also help developen of Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOS), since it will provide criteria for determining the responsiveness of an RTOS.

In this paper an implementation-independent Schedulability Analysis Tool (SAT) is presented. SAT has been designed in the context of the ESPRIT 111 OWCLEAR Omponents and Libraries for Embedded &plications in &al Time) project (partially funded by the European Union) [3,9). A prototype of the system has already been used in order to examine the schedulability, and thus the feasibility of certain embedded real-time applications coming from the white $oods and the automotive field (e.g., washing-machine and engine control).
The analysis supported by SAT is peaformed dwing the design phase of a hard real-time application.
The tool can also be used during the entire developmeat process, following the refinement/tunhg procedure.

This can be achieved by remodeling and refining the application and including the new effects that the underlying software (FZTOS or runtime support) introduces on the timing behaviour. Therefore, the tool does not present any additional overhead, from the first (approximated) version of the application, till the final and even the implemented one.

div.head: Approach
div.p: SAT determines a priori if a set of periodic and aperiodic real-time tasks (i.e., a real-time appIication) meets its timing requirements. In this way, SAT takes under consideration the designer's knowledge of the application's chatacterization data and the associated real-time requirements. These requirements include timing constraints, resource sharing and precedence relationships.

An appropriate approach to define the typical requirements that affect the schedulability analysis of a certain application is the one founded on an eventaction based framework [4]. In a real-time environment (apphcation plus Operating System), events (stimuli) are grouped into three categories, according to their origin: 0 environmental events: these are changes coming from outside the system (system environment) internal events: they result fkom changes occurring inside the system 0 timed events: they are a result of the passage of time.

In addition to that, events are characterized by their arrival pattern as follows: 0 periodic: events arriving at constant intervals (periods) 0 irregular: events arriving at prespecified, not constant intervals 0 bounded: events having a minimum arrival separation (bounded arrival pattern) bursty: when the number of events over a particular burst interval is restricted 0 unbounded: when each event arrivaI is desaibd in terms of a probability distribution function.
The analysis supported by SAT considers each aperiodic task as a periodic one, using the "urn interarrival time as its period (worstase scenario).

Every event has an associated response and sometimes responses are decomposed into smaUer segments of work called actions. This happens when the properties affecting the allocation of resources change during the response).

As far as resource constraints are concemed, SAT takes under consideration the blocking times caused by the exclusive sharing of resources. Furthermore, SAT takes into account the priorities, whidl define the precedence relationships among the tasks which constitute the real time application.
Moreover, the effects of the RTOS on which the application runs have to be considemi, in order to provide exact characterization for each application.

Operating Systems affect the timing behaviour ofa realtime application, since they add new events and actions (such as the clock signals and the context switch). The methods supported by SAT are sufficient to analyze these new effects. Consequently, the only responsibility for the SAT user is to obtain the necessary parameter values either fiom the system's docwnentaton or fiom the observation of the system behaviour (i.e., s t a n d a r d i z e d benchmarks can be used in order to derive the necessary parameters [2]).

div.p: The utilization U, associated with a periodic task t, is the mtio of the worst-case execution time C, over the period T, uf the task. The sum of all of the task utilizations is called the totai utilization for the set of tasks. The total utibtion is compared to the utilization bound, which is a theon%idly derived value [7]. A set of periodic tasks that uses static-prioriy scheduling and has total utilization equal to or less than the utilizaton bound is guaranteed to be schedulable.
